item.title: Dengue: 5 more die, 1,366 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Five people died of dengue, and 1,366 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours leading up to Tuesday morning.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 357 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the new deaths, two were reported in the Dhaka North City Corporation area and Barisal division each and one was recorded in Rangpur division, it said.
Of the total fatalities, 53.1% were female and 46.9% were male.
Since January 1 this year, hospitals across the country have admitted 115,617 dengue patients. Of them, 109,316 have recovered.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,204 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Tuesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,204.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,100, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
The three new suspected fatalities were reported across three divisions; Dhaka, Mymensingh, and Chittagong with one death each.
A total of 1,217 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Tuesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 215,768.
During the same period, 42 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,199.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 191,761 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 184,168 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: 30 Bangladeshis return home after release from Cambodia detention centre
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshi nationals who were released from an immigration detention centre in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, returned home on Tuesday.
They arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 12:15pm on a Thai Airways flight.
The returnees are Mohammad Harun Or Rashid, Mohammad Abdul Wadud, Mohammad Tarlib Hasan Titul, Sumit Chandra Das, Rakib Hossain, Bappi Das, Mohammad Labon Sheikh, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Mohammad Billal Hossain, Mohammad Mostafa, Nur Nabi, Mohammad Emon Ali, Mohammad Barkatullah, Mohammad Rubel Mia, Ali Ahmed, Zahidul Islam, Shamsul Alam, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Abu Jaher Sabuj, Shawon, Nahid Dhali, Raju Hossain, Mohammad Tayeb Ali Sheikh, Saimon Bhuiyan, Mohammad Rashedul, Mohammad Akash Ahmed, Mohammad Shimul Ali, Ashikur Rahman, Mohammad Alamin PK and Mohammad Kabir.
The Bangladeshis had travelled to Cambodia in search of jobs but became stranded at various scam centres in the country.
They registered to return home after the Cambodian government offered them the opportunity to leave without paying fines.
Accordingly, they arrived at Phnom Penh Airport on September 3. However, during immigration checks, Cambodian immigration police detained 32 Bangladeshis over various complications, including irregular immigration status.
Two were subsequently released, while the remaining 30 were held at the immigration detention centre.
Following an application by an organization named Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation, the first secretary of the labour wing at the Bangladesh Embassy in Bangkok was asked to take the necessary steps to secure the detainees’ release and facilitate their early return home.
After the required procedures were completed in phases, the 30 Bangladeshis returned to Bangladesh on Tuesday.

item.title: PM to visit Japan from October 26 to 29
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will pay an official visit to Japan from October 26 to 29 at the invitation of his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi to strengthen bilateral ties and expand economic cooperation.
The governments of Bangladesh and Japan formally announced the visit simultaneously on Tuesday.
“During the visit, the prime minister will hold high-level bilateral talks with Takaichi at her office on October 27,” Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam told journalists at a curtain raiser media briefing at the foreign ministry.
The Japanese premier will also host a luncheon in his honor, he added.
The foreign secretary said that the visit is expected to deepen the existing strategic partnership, attract fresh Japanese investment, expand trade and accelerate ongoing development projects.
Discussions will focus on the effective implementation of the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.
The two sides will also explore wider cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
The prime minister is scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.
His tentative program includes engagements with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation.
Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation.
The proposed itinerary includes visits to an LNG terminal and power plant in Futtsu City, Chiba, the headquarters of UNIQLO and a Toyota factory in Nagoya.
Announcements concerning memoranda of understanding or cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernization may be made during the visit, said the foreign secretary.
Detailed discussions are planned on Japanese support for establishing factories in Bangladesh, generating employment and developing human resources in line with the prime minister’s priorities.
Beyond bilateral matters, the two sides are expected to discuss regional and international peace and stability, a sustainable and peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis and stronger cooperation in addressing the energy crisis.
The prime minister will be accompanied by his spouse, Dr Zubaida Rahman, ministers, advisers, senior government officials and other delegation members.
The delegation will travel on Biman Bangladesh Airlines flights.
Japan, one of the first countries to recognize Bangladesh following independence, remains a major development partner, supporting infrastructure, human resource development and capacity building.
Its cooperation includes major projects such as the metro rail, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s Third Terminal and infrastructure development in Matarbari.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank sells another $20m to stabilize forex market
item.description:
Amid growing concerns that the US dollar exchange rate could cross the Tk124 mark, Bangladesh Bank has sold $20 million from the country's foreign exchange reserves.
The central bank sold this foreign currency to commercial banks on Monday, October 19, in an effort to keep dollar prices under control in the market.
A senior official of Bangladesh Bank confirmed the matter to the media.
This marks the second instance of dollar sales from the reserves in the current fiscal year. Earlier on September 14, the central bank had injected $11.5 million into the market.
On Monday, dollars were sold to commercial banks at a rate of Tk123.65 per dollar.
In comparison, the dollar was sold at Tk122.80 per dollar in September.
This indicates that Bangladesh Bank sold dollars at a rate Tk0.85 higher per dollar this time compared to the previous sale.

item.title: BFIU issues anti-money laundering guidelines for insurance companies
item.description:
The Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) has issued strict guidelines for all insurance companies in the country to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism.
Under the new directive, every institution must establish a central compliance unit, verify customer identities, detect and monitor suspicious transactions, and preserve necessary documents.
The instructions were issued through Bangladesh Bank on Monday.
According to the directive, every insurance company must formulate its own policy to combat money laundering and terrorist financing with approval from its Board of Directors or highest decision-making authority.
In addition, the chief executive officer must issue a clear commitment annually to employees and agents regarding this matter and take necessary measures to ensure proper implementation of the policy.
As per the BFIU guidelines, a central compliance unit headed by a senior official must be formed at the head office of each insurance company.
The Chief Anti-Money Laundering Compliance Officer (CAMLCO) will serve as the head of this unit, which will be responsible for supervising the institution's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing activities.
Furthermore, the central compliance unit must prepare an annual report covering progress, evaluations, and recommendations for activities from January to December of each year.
The report, along with the Chief Executive Officer's comments, must be presented at a meeting of the Board of Directors or the highest management committee, with a copy submitted to the BFIU by February of the following year.
The directive also mandates strengthening compliance operations at the branch level. A senior officer with at least three years of experience must be appointed as the anti-money laundering compliance officer in every branch and unit.
Similarly, designated officers must be nominated to oversee compliance for insurance agents as well.
These designated officers will be tasked with verifying customer identities, monitoring insurance policy transactions, identifying and reporting suspicious transactions, and maintaining relevant records, as well as ensuring necessary training for employees.
Regarding customer verification, no insurance policy can be opened or operated anonymously or under a pseudonym.
Opening or operating insurance policies in the name of individuals or entities listed under UN Security Council resolutions, or individuals and banned entities listed by the Bangladesh Government, is strictly prohibited.
The directive also clarifies the definition of a "customer" to include not only the policyholder, but also the ultimate beneficial owner of the policy and any person or entity operating a policy on behalf of another.
The BFIU issued these instructions using powers conferred under relevant provisions of the Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2012, and the Anti-Terrorism Act, 2009, with which all insurance institutions in the country must strictly comply.

item.title: India’s Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery
item.description:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio’s business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India’s purchases of Russian oil.
Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it’s a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India’s energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.
US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India’s continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
In February 2026, Trump announced a “trade deal” that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.
While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India’s deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India’s top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act,” imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the “C5+1” diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries,” he said.
“We’re trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that,” Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.
Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an “important node in global trade” because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.
Although Trump’s sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio’s decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.
“The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar,” she told DW. “The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue.”
Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance’s proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is “one of the states in play” in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
“Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome,” she said.
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defense, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
“Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values,” he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.
On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (Perm) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.
Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump’s own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
“Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians,” Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump’s presidency.
“The sense that America is unreliable, that America can’t be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse,” he said.
The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.
“If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals “will have consequences.”

item.title: UN: More than 250,000 displaced within Yemen since fighting flared
item.description:
More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the civil war reignited, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Yemen’s civil war -- in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis -- reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and then intensified when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Displacement is continuing to rise sharply across Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, which was already suffering a vast humanitarian crisis.
“UNHCR is obviously deeply concerned about the escalating displacement situation,” Matthew Saltmarsh, spokesman for the UN refugee agency, told a press conference in Geneva.
“The numbers displaced have now reached over 250,000.
“These are people who have been internally displaced in Yemen between August 1 and October 17.”
Around half of those newly displaced are being hosted in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognized government.
“The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance, said Saltmarsh.
The spokesman noted that as of Saturday, some 3,836 new arrivals had been recorded in Djibouti, and a further 242 in Somalia, including both refugees and returnees.
Following the capsizing of a boat travelling from Djibouti to Yemen on the night of October 8-9, 139 bodies have been recovered, including 109 who have been identified, he said.
Meanwhile 82 survivors have been identified and were receiving support.

item.title: UN says 19m Afghans facing acute food insecurity by April
item.description:
The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise to 19.2 million during the winter season between November and April, the United Nations said Tuesday.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of children in 2027, the UN humanitarian agency Ocha said.
Between September and October, 15.9 million people -- or nearly one in three Afghans -- were facing food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, including 3.4 million in emergency conditions, the agency said.
But the outlook is set to deteriorate further.
“The number facing acute food insecurity is projected to rise to 19.2 million, of which five million are expected to face emergency levels of hunger,” which is “one step away from famine,” said Ocha’s Afghanistan spokeswoman Olga Cherevko.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is not simply about whether the food is available, but also about whether people can afford it, she told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Kabul.
The latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification snapshot projects that more than four million children aged six months to five years old will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year.
“Over one million of these children are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition,” said Cherevko.
“These numbers represent children whose parents cannot afford nutritious food, and families whose ability to cope has been worn down by years of conflict, economic hardship, drought and other shocks.”
However, around one-third of nutrition sites across the country have closed or have suspended services, “largely due to funding cuts.”
“Once these services disappear, the consequences could be irreversible, particularly for children.”

item.title: Saudi says intercepted Houthi missile, blasts heard in capital
item.description:
Saudi forces on Tuesday said they had intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom’s capital, after authorities issued a danger warning and AFP journalists reported hearing blasts.
The kingdom “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh,” said Turki Al-Malki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition backing Yemen’s government in its war against the Houthis.
Riyadh was shaken by two blasts, according to AFP journalists in the capital.
“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert for a potential danger,” the Saudi civil defense said in a statement on X.
But the alert was lifted a few minutes later, with the civil defense saying “the danger has passed.”
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing the postponement of a major investment conference in a blow to Riyadh’s hopes of attracting greater foreign capital and diversifying its economy.
The deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis have forced Riyadh airport to shut.
The Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the group in retaliation amid fighting inside Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s Riyadh-backed government.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh’s control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before uprooting Yemeni government forces from positions along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign in September.

item.title: Body of Bangladeshi worker killed in Saudi airport attack to arrive Friday
item.description:
The body of Bangladeshi worker Md Shahed Ahmed, who was killed in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, will arrive in Bangladesh on Friday.
The body is scheduled to arrive at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 8:35am on a US-Bangla Airlines flight, according to a statement from the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh.
The statement said flight BS-362 will depart King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah for Dhaka at 11:10pm Riyadh time on Thursday, arriving in Dhaka at 8:35am the following day.
Shahed was killed in a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10. His father is Md Rafiqul Islam, and his home village is Madla in Shajahanpur upazila of Bogra.
He worked for Saudi Arabia-based Sa’ad Al Eisa Contracting Company at its Jeddah project. After spending a month on leave with his family, Shahed returned to Saudi Arabia on October 9 to resume work, leaving behind his wife and two children. The 36-year-old expatriate worker was killed while waiting for a transit connection at the airport.
Two Bangladeshis, including Shahed, were killed and at least 27 others injured in the attack. Most of the victims were waiting for connecting flights, either returning to their workplaces after visiting Bangladesh or travelling to perform Umrah.
Meanwhile, Shahed’s outstanding salary, allowances and service benefits, totalling 27,395.62 Saudi riyals (about Tk900,000), have been deposited into the Bangladesh Embassy’s account in Riyadh.
The money will be handed over to his family soon through the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board, the embassy said.

item.title: Gazette on Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026 issued
item.description:
The government has issued the Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026, allowing the establishment of solar power projects with a maximum capacity of five megawatts to accelerate the expansion of solar energy systems.
The gazette notification was issued on Monday.
The ordinance allows solar power projects on rooftops, courtyards, unused land and tea gardens, as well as floating and agrivoltaic systems.
It also prescribes imprisonment and fines for theft, vandalism, illegal connections and obstruction of solar power systems.
Solar power systems with a maximum capacity of five megawatts will be considered "special solar power systems" under the ordinance. However, large-scale ground-mounted solar power projects will remain outside its scope.
A tripartite agreement among the consumer, service provider and competent authority will be required for installing a special solar power system, following a government-prescribed standard contract template. The agreement will specify site-use rights, equipment standards, e-waste management, manufacturers' take-back schemes for discarded equipment, electricity tariffs and net-metering facilities.
A National Policy Council, headed by the prime minister, will be formed to oversee solar power expansion and policy coordination. Ministers or state ministers and senior secretaries from relevant ministries, including finance, law and power, will be members of the council.
District Technical and Coordination Committees, chaired by deputy commissioners (DCs), will also be formed, with superintendents of police, local engineers and district-level heads of power agencies as members. The committees will submit reports to the council every three months.
Meanwhile, Upazila Technical and Coordination Committees, led by upazila nirbahi officers (UNOs), will supervise field-level activities and report to the district committees every month.
The ordinance prescribes penalties for various offences to protect solar power systems. Theft of electricity or equipment, as well as buying, selling or possessing stolen goods, is punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of Tk50,000, or both.
Vandalizing or damaging solar panels or equipment carries a penalty of up to five years' imprisonment or a fine of up to Tk5,00,000. Illegal connections without written authorisation from the competent authority and obstructing personnel engaged in the installation, inspection or maintenance of solar power systems are punishable by up to three years' imprisonment or a fine of up to Tk5 lakh.
The ordinance also bars civil or criminal cases or other legal proceedings against the government, competent authorities or their officials and employees for actions taken in good faith under the ordinance, even if such actions cause or are likely to cause harm.

item.title: Trump says he wants Zelensky to “make a deal” with Russia
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday urged Volodymyr Zelensky to make a deal with Russia -- redoubling pressure on the Ukrainian leader even as Moscow grinds on with the war it launched four years ago.

Trump also said he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Stephen Hubbard -- an American taken captive by Moscow's forces years earlier in Ukraine -- in a fresh sign of his pivot back to Moscow.

"We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," Trump told reporters in the same room.

Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Zelensky had a bruising televised confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025, shortly after the Ukraine-skeptic US president returned to office.

"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump said Tuesday.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

The Ukrainian leader met Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks aimed at easing the tensions.

Zelensky hailed the resumption of US intelligence sharing on looming Russian strikes, but insisted Kyiv must be included in any future talks on its fate after meetings with US envoys.

Ukraine has been increasingly alarmed by Trump's return to effectively blaming Kyiv for a failure to end the war that began with Moscow's February 2022 invasion, and by his warm words towards Putin.

Trump indicated that a deal with Russia to free Hubbard could be near.

"I've been talking to President Putin about Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said in response to a question from an AFP journalist.

"Just stick with me," Trump added. "Just you remember that question a couple of days from now, because I do things that nobody else can do."

item.title: Lured to Russia by promises of jobs, 54 Bangladeshis killed in war in 3 years
item.description:
Abdullah Al Mamun of Lalmonirhat went to Russia hoping to secure a well-paying job and improve his family's financial condition. But his dream never came true. Instead, he ended up at a military camp after arriving in the country. The day before he was sent to the battlefield following training, Mamun called his younger brother Roni back home and said, "They are sending me to war. We may never see each other again. If we do not meet in this world, we will meet on the Day of Judgement."

Mamun's father, Abdul Majid, told Prothom Alo these words. He said he had not been able to contact his son since he was taken to the war. Later, Roni called Al Amin, who had travelled to Russia with Mamun. Al Amin informed him that Mamun had died.

A gayebana janaza was then arranged in their village. However, as his death had not been confirmed, people who came to attend the prayer did not perform the funeral prayer but instead offered munajat.

Five months have passed since then. The debt-ridden family is now helpless. Mamun's wife, who has a one-year-old son, has no idea how to move forward.

On 7 May, Mamun and 29 other Bangladeshis travelled from Dhaka to Russia in search of well-paid jobs. But after 21 days of training there, they were divided into groups of 16, eight and six and sent to the battlefield. Many of them reportedly died around 12 and 13 June. Two were admitted to hospital and later fled back to Bangladesh. They are Adnan Hossain of Narayanganj and Rajon Hossain of Jhenaidah. They provided information about the deaths of the others.

The number of Bangladeshis travelling to Russia has increased over the past few years. Many are being deceived and drawn into the Russia-Ukraine war. However, their bodies are not returned, nor are their deaths officially announced. Although they are officially listed as missing, their families know that they are dead. So far, at least 54 deaths have been reported over the past three years.

Adnan told Prothom Alo that Russia does not disclose information about the deaths of Bangladeshis in the war. Their bodies are not returned either. If someone does not return from the frontline, they are declared missing. But being missing means death. There is no other reason for return.

Adnan was admitted to a hospital in Moscow with shrapnel wounds to his abdomen after being injured on the battlefield. He underwent three surgeries and could not get out of bed for one and a half months. After spending two consecutive months in hospital, he fled to the Bangladesh Embassy. He then returned home on 15 September with a travel pass.

The Bangladesh Embassy in Russia has repeatedly raised objections to workers being sent without proper verification. In a letter sent by the embassy's labour wing to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment on 25 May, it said recruiting agency Jabal-E-Noor had sought permission on 5 May to send 70 workers, but the embassy did not attest to the documents.

The SRB, intelligence agencies and officials concerned said none of the Bangladeshis taken from the country was actually qualified to fight in a war. They lacked the physical fitness, training and tactical skills required for combat. Instead, they were primarily sent to the frontline and used as bait to identify enemy positions. When the opposing side launches drone attacks on them, Russian troops identify the enemy's positions.

Initially, RS International was supposed to bring 10 workers, but the process was suspended after suspicions arose. Later, on 18 May, a worker's family called the embassy and informed it that 30 people had travelled to Russia through Jabal-E-Noor and RS International and were being sent to the battlefield.

An investigation found that, as the two agencies failed to obtain attestation, the workers were sent under the name of TS Overseas.

The letter called for an investigation into the workers being sent without the embassy's approval. It also said a letter was being sent to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, requesting that the workers be brought back to the jobs specified in their employment contracts instead of being sent to war.

Bangladeshis sent to Russia for jobs, used as 'prey' in war, 20 killed: SRB

Sources from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the Russian government has been providing the Bangladesh Embassy with information about Bangladeshis reported missing or killed on the battlefield over the past four to five months. So far, Russia has provided details of 40 individuals, without specifying how many were killed and how many remain missing. The Russian authorities have yet to provide any information on the deaths of the latest 20 individuals.

Compensation may be claimed if someone dies in the war or remains missing for more than six months. However, obtaining compensation from Russia involves a complex process, including establishing the legal heirs and requiring the heirs to travel to Russia and stay there for at least six months. The bodies cannot be recovered either. Regular discussions are under way with Russia through diplomatic channels.

Russia has emerged as an important new labour market for Bangladesh. The number of workers being sent to the country began to rise mainly after the Russia-Ukraine war broke out in 2022. A network has been sending Bangladeshi workers to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war. Some regularly flee the battlefield and return home. Some die there, while others send messages pleading to be brought back to Bangladesh.

Bangladesh’s Ambassador to Russia, Md Nazrul Islam, told Prothom Alo that more than 90 per cent of the workers had gone to war of their own accord. Regarding the latest 30 individuals, the Russian side had also informed Bangladesh that they had joined the war voluntarily. Russia has written evidence to support this claim.

The Russian authorities are also refusing to hand over the bodies, making it impossible to bring them back to Bangladesh, he added.

No compensation without proof of death

Two organisations, Bangkok-based Fortify Rights and Ukraine-based Truth Hounds, said last March that 34 of more than 100 young Bangladeshis, who had joined the war in Ukraine on behalf of Russia, had been killed by that time.

At a press conference on 14 October, the Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 Bangladeshis had been sent to the battlefield in June after 21 days of training. The SRB had received information about the deaths of at least 20 of them.

Prothom Alo spoke to two men who returned home after being wounded and the families of six others. They said the men had pleaded with their families before being sent to the battlefield in June. When their families contacted the recruiting agency, it promised to take responsibility for them. However, they started going missing from the first week of June. Although their families received news of their deaths, they could not obtain any proof. The bodies of foreign nationals killed on the battlefield are not recovered; they are left there.

Deceived into fighting for Russia, Bangladeshi families now battle debt

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board said it takes responsibility for bringing home the bodies of migrant workers who die abroad. After a worker's death, their family must submit an application. If the worker had obtained clearance from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) before leaving the country or registered for membership with the embassy after going abroad, the board bears the cost of bringing the body home.

Even if neither of these conditions is met, the family can apply to the board. In that case, the board sends a proposal to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment. The ministry provides the funds to bring the body back to Bangladesh, with an allocation for this purpose included in the annual budget.

The board provides Tk 35,000 in cash assistance for the burial of each deceased worker whose body is brought back to the country. It then provides financial assistance of Tk 300,000. In addition, the worker's family is now entitled to life insurance benefits. If there are any compensation claims abroad, the embassy arranges to recover the money. The embassy also takes steps to recover any outstanding dues owed to the deceased worker.

However, the Welfare Board has not received any application so far to bring back the bodies of Bangladeshis from Russia. As there is no proof of their deaths, their families are unable to apply. As a result, none of them is receiving any compensation.

Pleas to return home

The SRB, intelligence agencies and officials concerned said none of the Bangladeshis taken from the country was actually qualified to fight in a war. They lacked the physical fitness, training and tactical skills required for combat. Instead, they were primarily sent to the frontline and used as bait to identify enemy positions. When the opposing side launches drone attacks on them, Russian troops identify the enemy's positions.

The SRB has also confirmed this in its preliminary investigation. Some manage to escape and return home when they get an opportunity to save their lives.

The SRB said the 30 Bangladeshis travelled to Russia on 7 May this year through three organisations — Jabal-E-Noor, RS International and TS Group. They were each charged an average of around Tk 1 million on the promise of jobs at construction companies. However, after arriving in Russia, they were handed over to the Russian military instead of being given the promised jobs.

Mizanur Rahman, founder of Jabal-E-Noor International, and Abu Taher, also known as Lentu, have been arrested as central figures in the human trafficking network.

Md Palash Sheikh was one of the 30 Bangladeshis. A group of 16 Bangladeshis was sent to the battlefield, and most members of the group are missing. Palash was wounded and admitted to hospital during his first deployment. During his second deployment, he lost an arm. He is now undergoing treatment at a hospital in Moscow.

His cousin Abu Saleh Islam told Prothom Alo that Palash Sheikh had been deceived by promises of a job and had been hospitalised for 22 days. Despite approaching the embassy and the ministry to bring him back home, the family had received no assistance.

Abu Saleh Islam further said that Palash Sheikh cannot even escape from the hospital because of the presence of armed guards. Although the family spent Tk 1 million to send him to Russia, they have received no money in return.

Prothom Alo has obtained 28 separate letters submitted by the families to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in July, seeking the return of their missing relatives.

The letters said the men had travelled to Russia through brokers in search of employment and a better life. Jabal-E-Noor International in Khilkhet and RS International in Ashulia had sent them to Russia. Lured by promises of high salaries, they were taken to Russia and handed over to the country's military.

The letters further said that preparations to send them to war had been completed and they could be forced to join the fighting at any time. The families urged the authorities to ensure their safe and speedy return to Bangladesh. They also sought financial assistance from the government.

Flow of workers to Russia continues

Rajon Hossain, 21, from Jhenaidah was among the group of 30 Bangladeshis who travelled to Russia on 7 May. Although he paid a broker Tk 1 million in the hope of getting a high-paying job, he never received one. After keeping him in a hotel for four days, the recruiters obtained his signature on a document and sent him to a military camp.

He told Prothom Alo that after 21 days of training, he was sent to the frontline along with five other Bangladeshis. Four of them were killed in drone attacks. Rajon was wounded and admitted to hospital, from where he escaped and returned to Bangladesh.

Earlier, Jahangir Alam from Lakshmipur was sent to Russia last year on the promise of a job as a cook at a military cantonment. He told Prothom Alo that he was handed a weapon and sent to the battlefield without any training. There were 16 of them in the group, and four were killed at the outset. He escaped from hospital and returned home.

Russia has emerged as an important new labour market for Bangladesh. The number of workers being sent to the country began to rise mainly after the Russia-Ukraine war broke out in 2022. A network has been sending Bangladeshi workers to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Some regularly flee the battlefield and return home. Some die there, while others send messages pleading to be brought back to Bangladesh. Yet the number of people travelling to Russia continues to rise.

According to data from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), only 37 people obtained clearance to travel to Russia in 2023. The figure rose to 1,395 the following year. In 2025, as many as 4,725 people obtained clearance to travel to the country. The number of workers going to Russia more than tripled in just one year. As of 15 October this year, some 3,105 people had obtained clearance to travel to Russia.

Shariful Hasan, head of the BRAC Migration Programme, told Prothom Alo that agencies accused of human trafficking are sending the highest number of workers to Russia.

According to him, no one knows how many have found jobs there or where the others are. Families are not even receiving the bodies of deceased workers, let alone compensation. No one knows how many have died, either.

Shariful Hasan suggested setting up a hotline to compile a list of missing Bangladeshis.

An agency sends 27pc workers

A Prothom Alo investigation found that, over the past four years, clearances had been issued in the names of 93 recruiting agencies to send workers to Russia. Among the three agencies accused by the SRB, one named TS Overseas obtained clearance for 266 workers. The names of the other two could not be found in the BMET database.

Bonna Bijoy Overseas obtained the highest number of clearances for sending workers to Russia. The agency alone accounted for 27 per cent of the workers, or nearly 2,500 people. It has faced allegations of human trafficking under the pretext of sending workers to Algeria, and there is also a human trafficking case against it. It has also faced allegations over sending workers to Russia. Despite this, clearances continue to be issued in its name.

Prothom Alo tried to contact Barun Debnath, managing director of Bonna Bijoy Overseas, but he did not answer the phone. He also did not respond to a text message.

According to BMET data, the government recruitment agency, Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), issued clearance for the second-highest number of workers, totalling 771.

A senior official at the agency told Prothom Alo that it had been sending workers to three Russian companies. However, several unfortunate incidents occurred. One worker fled with a vehicle, while another became involved in the war. Following these incidents, two of the companies stopped recruiting workers.

The official also said that workers are still being sent to the third company, with 14 more due to travel to Russia under an earlier demand letter. However, BOESL has not received any new demand letters for a year.

How trafficking network recruits workers

In November last year, the BRAC Migration Programme, a non-governmental development organisation, conducted a study on labour migration to Russia.

Based on testimonies from victims, statements from their families, documents and legal analysis, the study detailed a network involved in human trafficking and forced military recruitment under the guise of labour migration to Russia.

However, no one has an estimate of how many Bangladeshis have become involved in the Russia-Ukraine war, how many have been killed or how many remain trapped on the battlefield.

According to the BRAC report, young men are being taken to Russia with promises of well-paid jobs. Some are told they will work in factories, construction companies or the energy sector. But after arriving in Russia, some have their passports and mobile phones confiscated. They are then pressured and intimidated into signing documents to join the military before being sent to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield.

Some have returned home after being wounded, while others remain missing. Some families have received news of their relatives' deaths but have not been able to locate their bodies. At least 10 families approached BRAC with information about missing relatives. Some of them lost contact with their families after travelling to Russia in late 2024. Several other families received news of their relatives' deaths.

The deception began in Bangladesh itself. They had left the country with valid visas, employment contracts and all the necessary documents, only to be sent to the battlefield after arriving in Russia. According to CID sources, at least six cases have been filed over allegations of trafficking Bangladeshis to Russia.

Speaking about the issue, Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury told Prothom Alo that the government was discouraging workers from travelling in this manner. No one was being given clearance without verification and attestation of confirmed job information.

Stating that many people are travelling through different countries and using various means to reach Russia, the minister said, "All Bangladeshi embassies had been alerted and instructed to maintain contact with expatriate communities and monitor the situation."

Finding the bodies of those reported dead by their families is a difficult task, he said, adding that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was pursuing diplomatic efforts in this regard.

Yusuf Ali, Rajshahi Divisional Commissioner (additional secretary) has been withdrawn and attached to the Ministry of Public Administration. The authorities released him from his post with immediate effect on Tuesday. He left Rajshahi later that day.

Mohammad Rezaul Alam Sarkar, the additional divisional commissioner (Revenue), has been given responsibility as acting divisional commissioner.

The authorities have not specified the exact reason for Yusuf Ali’s immediate release from his post.

Asked about the matter, State Minister for Public Administration Md Abdul Bari told Prothom Alo on Wednesday that Yusuf Ali had been withdrawn for administrative reasons. “This happens all the time,” he said.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman visited Rajshahi on Tuesday. His flight landed at Shah Makhdum Airport in Rajshahi in the afternoon. He left Rajshahi at 7:00 pm after attending a public rally.

A video circulating on social media shows Divisional Commissioner Yusuf Ali leaning towards the Prime Minister and stepping forward while shaking his hand as he bade him farewell at the airport.

The footage appears to show him attempting to approach the Prime Minister by stepping out of the protocol line. The incident has sparked discussion over whether he breached official protocol.

Several sources at the Rajshahi Divisional Commissioner’s Office said the authorities had instructed Additional Secretary Yusuf Ali on Wednesday morning to report to the Ministry of Public Administration.

item.title: Trump confirms US-India trade deal finalisation soon
item.description:
US President Donald Trump has echoed Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicating that the bilateral trade agreement with India was close.

Speaking at a news briefing on Tuesday (local time), Trump was asked if the trade deal with India was close.

The US President replied, " They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah. Going to be a much different kind of a deal than we've made in the past."

Earlier, Rubio revealed that the India-US trade deal is “incredibly close”, indicating that finalisation is anticipated shortly.

Speaking to Network18, Rubio noted that while he is not directly engaged in the negotiations, which are handled through the trade representative, he has closely monitored the discussions and expects the agreement to materialise in a matter of weeks, not months.

“I’m not personally negotiating it; it’s done through our trade representative, but I know, and I’ve been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months,” said Rubio.

Elaborating on the meticulous final stages, he highlighted the necessity of absolute precision prior to public announcements to safeguard bilateral ties of such high importance.

“I felt that way before, and with these deals, it’s always important that it would be totally agreed to, every detail of it, before it’s announced because you can’t afford for a relationship of this magnitude to be threatened by announcing a deal and it turning out the deal wasn’t finalised. But it’s incredibly close. I think we are down to some technical details that need to be worked out. Technical details matter because there has to be an agreement; both sides have to agree that the language means the same thing. So, it’s down to that level,” he said.

Addressing queries concerning comparative rates for India alongside other nations, Rubio affirmed that the overarching outcome remains highly advantageous.

“The preponderance of it is good for you. And that’s what we aim to achieve here, and I can’t wait till we do it because we have so many things we can work together on,” Rubio stated.

Commenting on the sheer magnitude and diversity of the nation, the US Secretary of State underscored the necessity of broad exploratory visits rather than confining diplomatic engagements strictly to capitals.

“Well, this is a big country, it’s an important country, and I think like any big country, I say, people, if you want to learn and see what’s happening in the United States, you can’t just go to Washington. You should probably try to go somewhere in the South, maybe somewhere on the West Coast, and you probably need to get to New York, in Chicago. And so, for us, I mean, I don’t pretend that in my time as a Secretary of State I’ll get to see all of India, or learn about every region, but I think it’s important to see a country of this size and magnitude and to learn as much about it as you can,” Rubio remarked.

The India–U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement marks a major milestone in India’s global trade engagement, securing sustained preferential access for Indian exports in the U.S. market valued at over $30 trillion.

The agreement delivers comprehensive tariff rationalisation, zero-duty access across large product categories, enhanced digital and technology cooperation, and a carefully calibrated framework to safeguard India’s farmers, MSMEs and domestic industry.

item.title: Recruitment for 100,000 third and fourth class govt posts stalls
item.description:
Proposals to recruit staff for around 100,000 temporary posts in grades 16 to 20 across various government offices have been left pending.

Ministries and divisions cannot recruit for these third- and fourth-class positions because of revisions to the outsourcing policy. As a result, they cannot hire staff despite the demand, leaving members of the public deprived of essential services.

Until now, government offices recruited third- and fourth-class employees through outsourcing agencies or private companies. Under the revised policy, however, they can no longer recruit through private companies.

Ministries, divisions and government offices can recruit staff directly. Alternatively, a ministry or division may recruit through the Infrastructure Investment Facilitation Company (IIFC), a specialised organisation approved by the Finance Division.

The problem arose from the revision of the Service Procurement through Outsourcing Process Policy, 2025. The Ministry of Finance issued the policy on 21 September.

The revised policy allows government offices to obtain services directly from individuals instead of engaging private companies to provide outsourced services.

However, the Public Procurement Act and Rules contain no provision for procuring such services directly from individuals. Nor do the Public Procurement Rules (PPR) specify how ministries can directly recruit temporary staff for grades 16 to 20. Consequently, legal complications have emerged in implementing the new policy.

Since the revised policy came into force, various ministries and divisions have been unable to recruit third- and fourth-class employees through service-providing companies. At the same time, they cannot recruit the staff directly either.

Officials from various government departments and people familiar with the sector consider the policy incomplete and flawed. They say it does not clarify what will happen to ongoing tender processes for hiring staff through service-providing companies. Several ministries have written to the Ministry of Finance seeking a clear explanation of the matter.

Asib Ahsan, joint secretary of the Health Education and Family Welfare Division, told Prothom Alo that the division had asked the Ministry of Finance how it should handle ongoing tenders. His division plans to recruit several thousand service workers on a daily-wage basis. However, the lack of clarity in the policy has prevented it from proceeding with these appointments.

Since the revised policy came into force, various ministries and divisions have been unable to recruit third- and fourth-class employees through service-providing companies.

At the same time, they cannot recruit the staff directly either. In response to this situation, the Finance Division has written to the Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority (BPPA), requesting the necessary amendments to the Public Procurement Act and Rules. The Finance Division sent the letter on 21 September.

Recruitment stalls across various ministries

According to relevant sources at the Ministry of Finance, the new policy has stalled proposals to recruit staff for temporary posts under various ministries and divisions. These positions include hospital cleaners, laboratory assistants, trolley attendants and other service workers. The proposals also cover recruitment for cleaning and other support services at government residences and offices.

The revised policy allows government offices to obtain services directly from individuals instead of engaging private companies to provide outsourced services. However, the Public Procurement Act and Rules contain no provision for procuring such services directly from individuals. Nor do the Public Procurement Rules (PPR) specify how ministries can directly recruit temporary staff for grades 16 to 20.

Various institutions under the Ministry of Health have proposed recruiting around 20,000 service workers. Meanwhile, the Public Works Department plans to recruit around 5,000 employees to maintain government residences and offices. However, the new policy has prevented these recruitment processes from moving forward.

Relevant sources said similar situations had arisen in the Ministry of Railways, the Ministry of Social Welfare, the Ministry of Agriculture and several other ministries. Overall, recruitment proposals for around 100,000 temporary posts in grades 16 to 20 remain pending.

What is the Finance Division proposing?

In a letter dated 21 September, the Finance Division stated that it had revised the Service Procurement through Outsourcing Process Policy, 2025 to improve efficiency in government operations, ensure services are delivered in the shortest possible time, strengthen transparency and accountability, reduce public expenditure and procure quality services.

The letter stated that the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and the Public Procurement Rules, 2025, classify outsourcing as a physical service. However, neither the Act nor the Rules covers the procurement of such services directly from individuals.

The Finance Division therefore asked the Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority (BPPA) to take the necessary steps to incorporate provisions allowing the direct procurement of outsourced services from individuals into the Public Procurement Act and Rules, so that the revised policy could be implemented.

BPPA’s observations

In response to the Finance Division’s letter, the BPPA reviewed the proposal to procure outsourced services directly from individuals, along with the amendments the Finance Division had made to the policy.

In a letter to the Ministry of Finance dated 14 October, the authority stated that one of the main objectives of introducing outsourcing was to avoid direct contractual relationships between government offices and service workers.

Another objective was to prevent the financial and administrative complications that could arise if these workers later demanded inclusion in the government’s revenue budget.

Under the current system, the procuring authority signs a contract with a service provider selected through a competitive process. The service workers then provide services at government offices as employees of that company. However, allowing government offices to enter into contracts directly with individuals would fundamentally change the outsourcing framework. This could lead to the re-emergence of the complications that the existing system was designed to avoid.

The BPPA also noted that many individual service workers might lack the expertise required to follow and fulfil the prescribed contractual arrangements for providing services under the legal framework governing public procurement. As a result, implementing contracts directly with individuals could prove difficult.

The authority further warned that excluding private service providers could adversely affect the existing service sector. It could also raise questions about equal participation in public procurement.

The BPPA’s observations noted that barring private-sector participation in any government procurement process could conflict with the legal framework governing public procurement and international practices.

In addition, Rule 99(1)(b) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025, requires government-owned entities that provide physical services through direct contracts to deliver those services using their own personnel.

Therefore, the authority believes that the government should also consider the staffing levels, institutional capacity and potential conflicts of interest of the relevant public-sector organisations when assessing their ability to provide outsourced services nationwide.

The BPPA’s letter stated that the government should also review the methods used to select service workers, contractual liabilities and private-sector participation in a coordinated manner. The authority has therefore requested discussions involving the Finance Division, the BPPA and relevant stakeholders to determine the next steps.

2 opposing views on outsourcing

Opinions differ on whether government offices should recruit staff in grades 16 to 20 through private companies. Temporary employees recruited through private firms allege that they have to pay substantial sums to service providers before securing jobs in government offices.

Even after they start working, the companies deduct a portion of their monthly salaries. Describing the practice as a form of slavery, these workers have been demanding that the government recruit them directly.

Owners of private companies, however, argue that private recruitment allows them to train employees before assigning them to work. They also hold the workers accountable if any untoward incident occurs.

They contend that the government lacks the capacity to provide such training if it recruits employees directly. They also argue that holding workers accountable would be difficult if an untoward incident occurred under direct government recruitment.

Abu Taleb, president of the Bangladesh Outsourcing Manpower Provider Society, told Prothom Alo that private companies had recruited more than 500,000 workers for government institutions. He said the service providers were responsible for training, monitoring and ensuring accountability among these employees before and after recruitment.

The government now wants to recruit third- and fourth-class employees directly, he said, adding that this would increase disorder in government operations.

He also believes that direct recruitment would lead to more irregularities and corruption among government officials. Moreover, government institutions lack the capacity to recruit such a large workforce.

Why outsourcing recruitment was introduced

Sources at the Ministry of Finance said the government first introduced an outsourcing policy in 2008. At the time, the government argued that expenditure on salaries, allowances and pensions for public officials and employees was increasing and needed to be reduced.

To cut spending on various allowances and pensions, the government began recruiting workers for third- and fourth-class positions on a temporary basis from 2009, rather than appointing them directly to permanent government posts.

The policy stipulated that government authorities could not enter into contracts with individuals when procuring outsourced services. Instead, they had to sign contracts with recognised private companies. Authorities were also prohibited from issuing appointment letters in the names of individual workers.

The government subsequently revised the policy twice more, in 2018 and 2025.

How prepared is the state to protect Bangladeshi expats amid crisis in Saudi Arabia?
item.description:
The crisis in the Saudi Arabian labour market, airport attacks or security threats, flight cancellations, visa uncertainties, or the stranding of workers—each of these incidents raises a cruel question for Bangladesh: How prepared is the state to stand by the workers whose sweat enriches the country's foreign exchange reserves in times of trouble? Are we as diligent in ensuring the safety and future of migrant workers as we are in tracking the remittances they send?

This is not merely a question of administrative weakness; it is a question of state priorities, economic foresight, and the dignity of the citizen. We often call migrant workers the warriors of the economy and remittances the lifeblood of development.

Yet, when a crisis unfolds without an effective protection plan for them, a deep inconsistency manifests in this very philosophy of development. Can a state that considers the earnings of its citizens as national wealth ignore their personal misfortunes or sudden disasters?

Saudi Arabia is one of Bangladesh's most important labour markets. A large number of Bangladeshis work in various sectors such as construction, transportation, sanitation, and domestic work in Saudi Arabia. If employment there becomes restricted, recruitment policies change, or regional security situations deteriorate, thousands of families and the Bangladesh economy simultaneously come under pressure. However, over-reliance on a few labour markets, limited skills, and inadequate preparation for alternative employment have made our migration system vulnerable.

Have we ever accurately assessed at the national level how many workers would be affected if recruitment in Saudi Arabia decreased for a few months, how many families would lose income, and how many people would be unable to pay off loans? What alternative employment and financial security arrangements will be made if the crisis is prolonged? Without answers to these questions prepared in advance, one cannot escape responsibility citing unforeseen circumstances. Disasters may be sudden, but preparations to mitigate their damage are not made suddenly.

Finding an opportunity in a country's labour market and making one's future dependent on it are not the same thing. Bangladesh should consider the foreign labour market not just as a chance to send workers, but as part of national economic security. We become eager to send workers when demand increases in one or two Middle Eastern markets, but when the market contracts, there is a lack of long-term preparedness for alternative employment, rehabilitation, and financial security. As a result, labour migration has become largely an opportunistic system rather than a planned economic strategy. The goal of a farsighted state policy should be that a crisis in one market does not plunge thousands of people's futures into uncertainty.

When air travel is disrupted due to war or security threats, it is the workers who are most affected. These include those who have returned home on leave, workers going to join new jobs, and people stranded abroad. If flights are canceled, the cost of tickets is wasted, deadlines for joining jobs are missed, jobs are lost, visas expire, and the costs of accommodation and food increase, creating a risk of losing income. These situations are beyond the control of workers. Therefore, the government's responsibility is not only to inform about the situation but also to ensure effective solutions.

Ensuring reliable information is essential from the outset. Information on which airports are operational, which routes have flights, who are stranded where, and what assistance they need should be regularly updated. Without an integrated information system among embassies, consulates, airlines, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare, and relevant authorities, people will rely on rumours, fall into broker-traps, or move from one office to another seeking solutions.

The government should create separate lists for workers stranded in Saudi Arabia, those unable to return to work after coming home, and those waiting to travel with new employment. A coordinated digital database should be established by registering their location, visa duration, job contracts, employer's identity, outstanding salary, and financial liabilities.

Support priorities should be determined based on the type of problem through the exchange of information among embassies, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment, and Training (BMET), airlines, and recruiting agencies. It is important not only to know the number of affected individuals but also to regularly communicate how many problems have been resolved.

From the beginning of a crisis, multilingual hotlines, online registration, and emergency assistance desks need to be activated. Stranded workers should be provided with food, safe accommodation, medical, and legal assistance according to their needs. For those needing repatriation, coordination with the Saudi authorities and airlines is essential. Additionally, regular updates on flight status, alternative travel routes, and government guidelines must be provided to prevent them from falling prey to rumours or deception.

The most urgent requirement is negotiating with the Saudi authorities for visa extensions, job retention, or legitimate re-employment for those at risk of losing their visas or jobs. Direct communication with employers is necessary to ensure the return of workers stranded at home to their workplaces. For those waiting to embark on new jobs, arrangements should be made for ticket rescheduling, refunds, and alternative flights without additional costs. Initiatives to ensure alternative employment should be legitimate, verified, and consensual for the worker.

In addition, an urgent special fund for financial aid, food, accommodation, medical, and legal advice should be activated. Provisions for temporary loan payments, installment rescheduling, and financial aid according to the situation could be initiated for those who have taken loans to go abroad but are unable to join their jobs. The government needs to coordinate with financial institutions and relevant recruiting agencies. Flight cancellation news might be a headline for a day in the media, but for a worker's family, its financial implications could turn into a prolonged crisis.

A permanent emergency protection fund and risk-based work plan for expatriates is essential. Precisely what aid will be provided during war, pandemics, flight suspensions, or a sudden contraction in the labour market, who will perform what responsibility, and where the funds will come from should be predetermined.

During a crisis, an embassy's role should be a reliable sanctuary for citizens. Expatriates must not be left to find their path alone due to a lack of effective hotlines, updated instructions, grievance resolution, and emergency legal aid. Thus, adequate personnel and effective communication systems must be ensured in the labour welfare wing of embassies. Migrant workers should be under state protection not just during the period of foreign travel, but throughout their entire employment.

Most importantly, these initiatives must be integrated within a time-specific national work plan instead of remaining isolated administrative activities. For each grievance of an affected worker, a tracking identification number should be implemented, notifying the worker and their family about which officer is responsible, when the resolution will occur, and what progress has been made.

It is more important how many workers' jobs have been saved, how many visas have been extended, how many have received back wages, and how many families have received emergency aid than how many meetings the government has held. The real measure of administrative action is not the number of meetings, statements, or assurances but the tangible solutions to the affected workers' problems. Transparency in crisis management is not an additional courtesy; it is a fundamental responsibility of a state operating on public funds.

The ongoing crisis in Saudi Arabia warns us: Will we revert to old dependencies with temporary initiatives each time, or will we establish alternative markets, skills, social security, and accountability systems? Crises will eventually pass. But if there is a lack of preparation and over-dependence on a single market, the same situation will recur in subsequent crises.

It must be remembered that a migrant worker is not a remittance machine; he or she is a citizen, the last hope for a family. If the state merely observes the situation during a time of danger, the claims of development remain incomplete. Crises will come, but leaving the citizen alone is not inevitable. It is a test of preparation, policy priority, and state accountability. The expatriate's money is the country's wealth; their life is the state's responsibility.

#Dr. Selim Reza, Associate Professor & Coordinator, Centre for Migration Studies (CMS), North South University.

item.title: Bangladesh eyes wider South American market as exports reach $195m
item.description:
Bangladesh’s exports to 11 South American markets reached $195.17 million in the first quarter of the current FY27, as the government stepped up efforts to diversify export destinations through trade fairs and the promotion of non-traditional products.
According to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data, Bangladesh exported goods worth $195.17 million to the region during July-September of FY27, with Brazil, Chile and Peru emerging as the three largest destinations.
Brazil topped the list with $70.82 million, followed by Chile with $51.87 million and Peru with $24.24 million. Colombia accounted for $18.05 million, while exports to Uruguay and Argentina stood at $11.63 million and $10.28 million, respectively.
The figures highlight South America’s potential as a market for Bangladeshi products beyond the country’s traditional destinations in Europe and North America.
Readymade garments continued to dominate the export basket. However, Bangladesh’s recent participation in Home Show Brazil 2026 in São Paulo also highlighted opportunities for jute goods, leather products, home décor, handicrafts and other lifestyle products.
Brazil fair opens doors for diversified exports
Bangladesh participated in Home Show Brazil 2026, held from August 11 to 13 at Distrito Anhembi in São Paulo, with financial support from the EPB and under the management of the Bangladesh Embassy in Brasília.
Four Bangladeshi companies—Jihan Plastic Industries, Mother Tannery, Rainbow Jute and Classical Handmade Products—showcased their products at five booths at the exhibition.
Their displays included jute goods, bags, leather products, natural-fibre baskets, home décor items, bamboo products, terracotta, clay products and Nakshi Kantha.
The EPB and the Bangladesh Embassy also operated a promotional booth featuring information on Bangladesh’s exportable products and key export sectors.
Business-to-business meetings were held during the fair, while prospective buyers visited the Bangladeshi stalls and expressed interest in the products on display.
A seminar on the production and export of home and lifestyle products from Bangladesh was also organized as part of the fair to promote the country’s products among Brazilian business organizations and international buyers.
EPB stresses market diversification
EPB vice chairman and chief executive Mohammad Hasan Arif said the bureau was working to diversify Bangladesh’s export basket and strengthen the country’s presence in emerging international markets through more strategic and professional participation in trade fairs.
He said excessive dependence on readymade garments and a limited number of export destinations could expose Bangladesh’s export earnings to external shocks, making product diversification and market expansion increasingly important.
Arif stressed that exporters should conduct advance research into market demand, consumer preferences, pricing, competition and business practices before participating in international exhibitions to achieve better commercial outcomes.
He also underscored the importance of strengthening national pavilion branding, improving exporters’ preparedness and engaging directly with international buyers to turn trade-fair participation into sustainable business opportunities.
RMG remain main export driver
Bangladesh’s export basket to the 11 South American markets remains heavily concentrated in apparel.
According to product-wise figures from the EPB spreadsheet, exports of woven apparel and clothing accessories amounted to around $84.53 million during July-September, while shipments of knitted or crocheted apparel stood at approximately $70.10 million.
Together, the two categories generated around $154.63 million, equivalent to nearly 79.2% of total exports to the 11 markets.
Pharmaceutical products contributed around $6.58 million, while footwear and related products accounted for approximately $5.71 million.
Other textile products, leather goods and travel articles also featured in the export basket, indicating scope to expand the range of products sold in the region.
Brazil and Chile together accounted for $122.69 million, or nearly 62.9%, of total exports to the 11 markets.
Their importance makes them key destinations for targeted export promotion, while Peru and Colombia also offer opportunities for further commercial engagement.

item.title: ADB: Urgent adaptation needed to save Bangladesh’s coastal delta, economy

As the Asian Development Bank (ADB) released its flagship Asia–Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise—Actions for a Resilient Future , the findings hit home sharply for Bangladesh.
While coasts across the region generate $7 trillion in annual economic output, they are retreating rapidly under the weight of rising seas and intensifying hazards.
For a deltaic nation where millions live within low-elevation coastal zones vulnerable to tidal surges, cyclones, and soil salinity, the report underscores an urgent reality: adaptation is no longer optional; it is an economic and existential imperative.
Across 30 coastal economies evaluated in the report, annual flood damages could skyrocket from roughly $27 billion today to between $172 billion and $199 billion by 2050, and surge up to $739 billion by 2100 under high-emissions scenarios if adaptation measures stall.
For Bangladesh, regional trade hubs like Chattogram and Mongla face severe risks. Across the wider Asia-Pacific, port disruptions alone put $40 billion to $45 billion at risk annually.
