item.title: Bangladesh improves in rule of law index but trails several African nations
item.description:
Bangladesh has made a slight improvement in its overall rule of law score but continues to rank below several African countries, including Kenya, Zimbabwe and Nigeria, according to the Rule of Law Index 2026 released on Wednesday.
Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index, behind Zimbabwe (122nd), Nigeria (120th), Sierra Leone (110th), Liberia (103rd), Kenya (100th) and Ghana (62nd).
Its score increased by 0.6% to 0.393 out of 1, up from 0.391 in 2025, making Bangladesh the world's 15th-biggest improver and South Asia's top gainer. Its ranking improved by two places from 125th, although its score remained below the global average of 0.55.
The index assesses countries across eight factors: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice.
Bangladesh improved in only three factors — constraints on government powers, absence of corruption and regulatory enforcement — while its performance declined in the other five.
Fundamental rights remained the country's weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 133rd and scoring 0.30, placing it among the 11 lowest-ranked countries.
The indicator assesses the protection of fundamental human rights under international law. Civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36. The indicator measures access to and the effectiveness of the civil justice system in resolving grievances.
Bangladesh ranked 124th in regulatory enforcement, with a score of 0.40, and 117th in criminal justice, scoring 0.32. In the absence of corruption category, which measures bribery, improper influence and the misappropriation of public resources, it ranked 113th with a score of 0.35.
The country ranked 111th in constraints on government powers, which measures accountability under the law, with a score of 0.38.
Open government was Bangladesh's highest-ranked factor at 106th, with a score of 0.41. It assesses government transparency, accountability mechanisms and public participation in policy deliberations.
Bangladesh ranked 107th in order and security, scoring 0.63. The factor measures how effectively a society protects individuals and property.
Despite the annual improvement, Bangladesh's overall rule of law score declined by 0.8% between 2021 and 2026, falling from 0.40 to around 0.39, according to the WJP's country profile.
Six of the index's eight factors deteriorated over the five-year period. Civil justice recorded the sharpest decline at 4.2%, followed by open government at 2.8%, fundamental rights at 1.5%, regulatory enforcement at 0.9%, criminal justice at 0.7% and absence of corruption at 0.2%.
Constraints on government powers and order and security improved by 2.3% and 0.6%, respectively.
Human rights activist and Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Jyotirmoy Barua attributed the deterioration partly to the worsening law and order situation.
"We had expected that an elected government would be able to turn things around to some extent, as the interim government had failed to maintain or restore control over the law and order situation," he said.
"However, the elected government has been trying to bring the entire situation under control at once, and the pressure associated with this has contributed to instability. Law enforcement is also closely linked to the justice system, and our overall performance in these areas has deteriorated," he added.
Nepal remained South Asia's top performer, ranking 71st globally with a score of 0.52, followed by Sri Lanka at 74th and India at 88th. Bangladesh ranked ahead of only Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd) in the region.
Denmark topped the 2026 index, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg. Venezuela ranked last, preceded by Afghanistan, Haiti, Cambodia and Nicaragua.
The index drew on data from more than 215,000 households and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts across 143 countries and jurisdictions. The data were collected between February and August 2026.
The WJP highlighted the links between the rule of law and economic prosperity. Countries with GDP per capita above the global average of $14,406 scored at least 0.68 on the index, while those with inflation below the global median of 3.23% scored at least 0.60. The findings indicate an association between the rule of law, price stability and economic performance.

item.title: PM tours Sundarbans by helicopter, travels to Mongla via Dacope

item.title: UPDF opens fire on tourists, law enforcement personnel in Rangamati's Sajek: ISPR
item.description:
Armed members of the United People's Democratic Front (UPDF) opened fire on tourists and law enforcement in the Gangaram Bazaar area of Sajek, Rangamati district, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The ISPR stated in a press release that the UPDF forcibly used local residents as human shields to block roads.

As a result of the blockage on the Sajek-Baghaihat road, about three thousand tourists visiting Sajek were stranded.

The ISPR press release mentioned that while ensuring the safe passage of tourists, the blockaders created obstacles. In this situation, the Bangladesh Army and police jointly took necessary security measures to ensure the tourists' safe transport to Khagrachari.

While removing the stranded tourists, around 10 AM on Thursday, the blockaders erected barriers in the Gangaram Bazaar area, halting the movement of tourist vehicles. At that time, the army and police patrol team initiated discussions with the blockaders to ensure the safe passage of tourists.

However, during the discussions and around 10: 45 AM, the blockaders, incited by the UPDF, suddenly started throwing stones at law enforcement and targeting tourists, as noted in the statement. To bring the situation under control, the law enforcement used baton charges to disperse the blockaders and resumed the movement of tourist vehicles.

According to the ISPR statement, at approximately 11 AM, it was initially learned that armed UPDF members fired about 30-40 rounds at law enforcement and tourists. During this time, the army patrol team, in self-defense and to ensure the safety of tourists, returned fire, causing the armed individuals to flee the scene. Subsequently, with coordinated efforts by the Bangladesh Army and police, the trapped tourists were evacuated safely, and no casualties were reported.

Preliminary information suggests that the blockade and violence instigated by the UPDF were premeditated. The allegations that locals were coerced into participating in the blockade and being used as human shields are extremely concerning, as mentioned in the statement. It was stated that, due to ongoing security operations in various parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, a faction of UPDF's armed members has taken position in the tourist area.

The statement noted that such violent activities disrupt peace, stability, and public safety in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and adversely affect the tourism industry and the livelihoods of local people. Especially alarming are incidents endangering the safety of innocent tourists and forcibly involving the general public in the blockade program.

The Bangladesh Army continues its efforts in coordination with the civil administration and other law enforcement agencies to maintain peace, harmony, and stability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and to ensure the safety of the lives and property of local residents and tourists. ISPR informed that the Bangladesh Army will continue its efforts to maintain the peaceful environment of the hill region in the future.

Notably, yesterday, Wednesday, the Sajek Jan Adhikar Raksha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association announced a blockade for the third time on the Sajek tourism road. According to a statement from the organisations, the blockade would continue indefinitely starting today. Therefore, tourists were requested to leave Sajek by yesterday, Wedenday.

Following the blockade call by these regional organisations, the district administration announced the closure of Sajek for safety reasons.

In a public notice last evening, Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi stated that the Sajek Valley tourist center in Baghaichhari Upazila would remain temporarily closed until further notice.

item.title: Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
item.description:
FIJI-UN-COP31-CLIMATE-ENVIRONMENT

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an "extremely high risk" of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.

In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" -- its highest risk category.

Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.

For their assessment, researchers used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned Wednesday.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.

Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.

The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems.

Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.

Critically endangered coral

The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered -- Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.

A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals -- which build its living foundation -- largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

The report was released during the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world "are not yet lost".

If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24 percent of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96 percent, the IUCN said.

"It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming," said IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar.

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them."

A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at "elevated relative risk of extinction", with climate change the main driver of this decline.

item.title: PHP security flaw triggers global cyber alert, millions of websites at risk
item.description:
Bangladesh e-Government Computer Incident Response Team (BGd e-GOV CIRT) has issued a high-severity alert over two critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites and web applications.
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed “PHP2Shell”, could allow hackers to remotely run malicious code on vulnerable servers without a username or password, potentially giving them control of affected systems.
The flaws, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, carry a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of 9.2 out of 10, placing them in the critical severity category.
According to the alert, the vulnerabilities stem from PHP’s memory management. Attackers could exploit situations involving memory exhaustion or data persisting from previous requests after memory is freed by sending specially crafted HTTP requests to gain control of a server.
Users of PHP-FPM and Apache’s mod_php are particularly at risk. Other potentially affected systems include PHP-CGI, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Docker containers and shared hosting environments. Government portals, banks, e-commerce platforms and websites built on WordPress and Laravel could also be vulnerable.
A successful attack could result in full server compromise, data and file theft, exposure of database passwords and API keys, and website outages, the alert warned.
BGD e-GOV CIRT has urged administrators to update PHP immediately to the secure versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. It also advised them to ensure that the server’s underlying PHP runtime is updated, not just the application framework.
For administrators unable to install the patches immediately, the agency recommended temporarily placing servers behind a VPN, restricting access through IP-based allowlists and increasing log monitoring.
However, BGD e-GOV CIRT stressed that updating PHP is the only permanent solution.

item.title: Dhaka-Chittagong rail services resume after 24 hours
item.description:
Train services on the Dhaka-bound line of the Dhaka-Chittagong route resumed at 12:50pm on Thursday, more than 24 hours after the Karnaphuli Commuter Express derailed in Comilla's Laksam.
The Bijoy Express, travelling from Chittagong to Mymensingh, was the first train to cross the accident site after the line reopened.
Omar Faruk Bhuiyan, station master of Laksam Railway Junction, said train services were now operating normally on both lines.
The damaged track was repaired by 7am on Thursday, but services remained suspended on the Dhaka-bound line because a derailed coach was found. During the suspension, trains in both directions used the other line, causing some disruption. The Chattala Express, bound for Dhaka, and the Paharika Express, bound for Sylhet, passed through Laksam at 10:23am and 10:48am, respectively, on Thursday.
The accident occurred around 12:30pm on Wednesday in the outer section of Naoti station, near Azgara Bazar in Laksam, when five coaches of the Karnaphuli Commuter Express and three wheels of its engine derailed. At least seven passengers were injured.
A rescue train from Chittagong reached the site on Wednesday evening. Recovery work was completed around 5am on Thursday, followed by track repairs.
Meanwhile, railway authorities suspended sub-assistant engineer Sarwar Alam over allegations that he failed to inform the control room about repair work underway at the accident site. He was responsible for the Feni region under the Eastern Railway’s engineering department.
A four-member committee has been formed to investigate the accident, Chittagong Divisional Railway Manager Mostafizur Rahman Bhuiyan said on Wednesday night.

item.title: 4,157 killed in nine months as nation marks Road Safety Day
item.description:
Twelve people died in a head-on collision in Natore on Tuesday. According to police and surviving passengers, the bus was being driven by its supervisor while the regular driver slept in the back.
Two days later, Bangladesh is observing National Road Safety Day with the familiar program of seminars, discussions and promises to make its roads safer.
The latest figures offer little reason for reassurance.
At least 4,157 people were killed and 5,391 injured in 4,285 road crashes between January and September this year, according to the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA). That is an average of more than 15 deaths every day.
This year’s observance, under the theme “Safe Roads, Prosperous Nation, Bangladesh First,” comes amid persistent concerns over unfit vehicles, unqualified drivers and the failure to enforce existing traffic laws.
The Natore crash brought several of those concerns into sharp focus.
Police and injured passengers said the RP Special Paribahan bus was heading towards Bonpara when its supervisor, Sohel Rana, took over the wheel after a stop at Ishwardi around 3am.
Ramjan Ali, a surviving passenger from Chapainawabganj, said the regular driver left his seat after the break. About an hour later, the bus collided with a truck, killing 12 people and injuring at least 25.
The circumstances of the crash have once again raised questions about who is allowed to drive passenger buses and how effectively transport operators are monitored.
The deaths in Natore are part of a much larger toll.
According to Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity, at least 125,405 people were killed in 72,736 road crashes between 2013 and 2025. Another 176,249 people were left permanently disabled, the organisation said.
Children have been among the worst affected. Road Safety Foundation figures show that 7,963 children died in road crashes between January 2020 and September 2026.
Nearly 3,000 of them were killed in motorcycle crashes, while 2,812 died as pedestrians.
Yet the problems identified by successive governments and road safety experts remain largely unresolved.
BRTA records indicate that around 650,000 vehicles are operating without the required registration, route permits or fitness certificates. More than 75,000 buses and trucks have exceeded their prescribed economic lifespan.
The shortage of qualified professional drivers for heavy and medium vehicles is estimated at around 30%.
Vehicle fitness is another major concern. Around 70% of buses and minibuses in Dhaka and other major cities reportedly lack valid fitness documents.
Driver health also receives inadequate attention. At a BRTA and Dhaka Ahsania Mission health camp in 2023, around 73% of 541 drivers who underwent eye examinations were found to need glasses.
In 2019, the National Road Safety Council identified seven priority areas and made 111 recommendations to improve road safety.
Experts say there has been little visible progress in implementing them.
BUET Assistant Professor Kazi Md Saifun Newaz said the country already has the Road Transport Act 2018 and Road Transport Rules 2022, but legislation alone cannot prevent crashes.
“Everyone knows the causes of road crashes and their remedies. What is missing is consistent and coordinated action,” he said.
“Observing days will not solve anything.”
The BRTA says it has filed more than 110,000 cases through mobile courts and joint enforcement drives in the first nine months of this year, targeting unfit vehicles, invalid licences, speeding and other violations.
But the continuing death toll raises questions about whether these drives are producing lasting improvements.
Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity Secretary General Mozammel Haque Chowdhury blamed institutional inefficiency, corruption and the influence of transport owners’ and workers’ groups for the persistent disorder.
Road Safety Foundation Executive Director Saidur Rahman said the dangers were particularly acute for children on rural roads, where vehicles frequently pass close to homes and enforcement is weak.
“The authorities know the causes and the consequences, but there is no remedy,” he said.
The government has pledged to enact a comprehensive road safety law by December 2027.
The proposed Road Safety Act 2026 includes free emergency treatment for crash victims, legal protection for people who assist the injured, a demerit-point system for traffic offenders and higher penalties for repeat violations.
Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam has also reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to the UN target of halving road deaths and serious injuries by 2030.
For now, the country enters another Road Safety Day with thousands of lives lost, longstanding recommendations awaiting implementation and another deadly crash exposing the dangers on its highways.

item.title: Govt to ease capital repatriation, boost investor confidence
item.description:
The government has planned to introduce a 30-day deadline for processing applications to repatriate profits from lawful foreign investments, alongside a series of financial reforms aimed at reducing business costs and strengthening investor confidence.
The proposed measures, outlined in a budget document, seek to address administrative bottlenecks affecting foreign investors while making banking services, foreign trade transactions and access to financing more efficient.
The document says coordination among banking verification, tax-related documents and approval processes will be strengthened to ensure timely processing of profit repatriation applications.
The government has also simplified the repatriation and reinvestment of proceeds from shares or securities purchased through a Non-Resident Investors’ Taka Account (Nita).
The requirement for an auditor’s certificate has been withdrawn, allowing such proceeds to be credited directly to the relevant Nita.
This will enable repatriation and reinvestment within one working day and reduce compliance costs.
Share transfers and capital repatriation involving unlisted companies will also become easier. No valuation report will be required for transactions worth up to Tk1 crore, while repatriation of transaction proceeds of up to Tk100 crore will be allowed without prior approval from Bangladesh Bank.
For larger transactions, licensed valuation firms will be introduced to ensure more neutral and acceptable share valuations.
The government is also considering a certification board comprising representatives from Bangladesh Bank, the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (Bida), the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC), the National Board of Revenue and the private sector.
Acceptance of reports from approved valuation firms could reduce repeated verification and delays in capital repatriation.
To cut the time and cost of foreign trade, the government will consider gradually relaxing the mandatory use of letters of credit for reliable importers and low-risk goods.
The use of Documents against Payment (D/P) and Telegraphic Transfer (TT) will be expanded where appropriate.
Companies registered in Bangladesh will also be able to obtain loans in taka against foreign bank guarantees or Standby Letters of Credit (SBLC), regardless of their ownership or control structure, subject to applicable rules.
The requirement for separate prior approval for each loan from an Offshore Banking Unit (OBU) will be reviewed.
However, existing provisions on Credit Information Bureau reporting, single-borrower limits, loan classification and provisioning will remain in force.
The approval process for renting, leasing, renewing and relocating bank branches and business centres has also been simplified.
Within prescribed region-wise rent ceilings, banks may take such decisions with approval from their boards of directors.
The government has further simplified the process of obtaining a Sukuk Investor ID (SIID) for investment in government Sukuk by determining the required application forms, documents and fee structures.
To expand digital financial services, Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) will be made more effective, with faster payment and settlement arrangements among banks, mobile financial service providers and other payment platforms.
The document says the introduction of digital small loans, or e-Loans, has been permitted.
Loans of up to Tk5 lakh may be provided for 12 months through a fully digital process to improve access to credit and reduce customers’ time and operational costs.
Pre-suit mediation has also been encouraged for recovering defaulted loans to reduce court-related delays and expenses and improve recovery efficiency.
The government has relaxed lending rules for environment-friendly vehicles and personal financing.
The maximum auto loan for electric and hybrid vehicles has been increased from Tk60 lakh to Tk80 lakh, while the debt-equity ratio has been raised from 60:40 to 80:20.
The ceiling for unsecured personal loans has been doubled from Tk5 lakh to Tk10 lakh, while secured personal loans may now be provided up to Tk40 lakh.
Credit card limits have also been increased. The maximum limit for unsecured credit cards has risen from Tk10 lakh to Tk20 lakh, while the limit against securities has increased from Tk20 lakh to Tk40 lakh.
Banks may introduce new credit cards with approval from their boards of directors without obtaining prior approval from Bangladesh Bank.
The document says the measures are intended to reduce administrative complexity and costs across investment, foreign trade, banking and lending, while strengthening investor confidence, financial inclusion and the growth of the digital economy.

item.title: Excess liquidity in banking industry reaches Tk442,000cr
item.description:
Surplus liquidity in the country's banking sector has increased, reaching Tk442,000 crore.
Due to sluggish credit demand in the private sector, banks are disbursing less money as loans compared to the deposits they receive.
Consequently, idle money is accumulating, and the advance-deposit ratio (ADR) is on the decline.
According to Bangladesh Bank's "Major Economic Indicators" report for September, the total liquidity of the banking sector stood at Tk7,81,214 crore at the end of last August.
Against this, the statutory minimum liquidity requirement was Tk339,260 crore.
As a result, the surplus liquidity stands at Tk441,954 crore.
According to the report, conventional private commercial banks hold the highest amount of surplus liquidity.
At the end of August, the surplus liquidity in these banks stood at Tk271,691 crore.
Meanwhile, state-owned commercial banks held surplus liquidity worth Tk140,835 crore.
However, this liquidity is not distributed evenly across all banking institutions.
Due to irregularities and weak financial positions, several banks continue to suffer from a liquidity crisis.
On the other hand, the credit-to-deposit ratio (advance-deposit ratio) in the banking sector is continuously dropping.
Bangladesh Bank data reveals that the ratio was 80.38% at the end of December 2023.
Although it rose to 81.32% in September 2024, it later began to decline.
By September 2025, it dropped to 78.28%, and by the end of December that year, it fell further to 77.72%.
By the end of March this year, it stood even lower at 75.80%.
According to bankers, as private sector credit demand remains weak, banks are unable to accelerate new loan disbursements as expected.
Consequently, a portion of the surplus money is being invested in government treasury bills and bonds, while some funds remain idle in bank accounts.

item.title: Ukraine and Russia trade strikes following Witkoff talks
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, authorities from both countries said on Thursday, shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding tens of residents, city authorities said.
In an update later in the morning, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had fired 21 missiles towards 12 regions in Ukraine. In Kyiv region, the strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, including five children.
The subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv was also damaged, Mayor ⁠Vitali ​Klitschko ​said ​on Telegram.
“Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential Areas,” Ukrainian foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
His post referred to Witkoff recently calling Putin a “humanitarian” for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday. Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces and jailed over charges of being a mercenary.
The Ukrainian foreign minister added: “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Another Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the Poltava region, local authorities said without providing more details.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, with many targeting Moscow.
At least two people were killed in the Ukrainian strikes on Russia.
In western Russia’s Lipetsk city, a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on Telegram.
The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Zelensky in Norway earlier this week, followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has attempted to mediate between the two sides to end the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Putin agreed “in principle” to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. Zelensky, too, said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for trilateral talks at the negotiators level to be held as soon as possible.
It was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff’s meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks.
“Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” Zelensky said in a post on social media on Thursday.
“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing,” he said, once again advocating for stronger air defense capabilities and a faster supply of missiles from allies.

item.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
item.description:
At least two people were killed in a strike on a Saudi airport in the eastern city of Dammam on Wednesday, as Washington ordered some diplomats and family members to leave the Gulf country.
Saudi Arabia’s revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports.
The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed two people and injured eight others.
The authority added on X that the extent of the material damage to the airport was being assessed.
It did not say who was behind the attack and the Houthis did not claim responsibility.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said flights from the airport were being diverted as operations came to a halt.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said forces successfully intercepted a drone targeting an oil facility, but that falling debris killed two people and injured two others. Those killed were identified by the ministry as a Filipino and a Nepali national.
Meanwhile, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said his department had issued an order for the departure of non-essential staff and family members at the US embassy in Riyadh.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” Pigott wrote on X.
Both Reuters and AFP news agency cited unnamed sources as saying a similar order was also issued for other countries in the Gulf, with the AFP listing the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain.
Pigott denied the reports, saying they were “inaccurate” and that only employees in Saudi Arabia were ordered to leave.
The US has issued similar evacuation orders on more than one occasion this year amid the Iran war and Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Tehran.
A four-year truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels collapsed amid the Iran war, with Saudi Arabia experiencing near daily attacks this month.

item.title: Son of Myanmar’s Suu Kyi says had first call in five years
item.description:
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.
Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
AFP could not immediately reach Aris -- who lives in the United Kingdom -- and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.
However, he posted images accompanying his Facebook post which appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.
“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military held Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.
But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.
On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.
Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing -- who ousted Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup -- was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks
item.description:
The official website of Bangladesh Bank has been kept offline due to concerns over a possible cyber-attack.

However, internet banking and mobile banking transactions are functioning normally, so customers are not facing any issues with their transactions.

Regarding this, Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arif Hossain Khan told Prothom Alo on Thursday night that the website is being checked for any faults.

This decision was made due to concerns about worldwide attacks. There are no problems for customers in their transactions as a result.

Currently, the internet and software are extremely important for delivering government services, banking, e-commerce, media, and various online platforms.

A significant portion of these websites relies on the PHP programming language. Recently, after two critical security flaws were identified in PHP, there has been global concern about cyber security.

According to BBC and Reuters reports, after two critical security flaws were found in PHP, a widely used programming language for developing and managing websites, various governments have taken emergency actions.

Following the news of the flaws, governments and commercial enterprises worldwide have shut down their websites since Wednesday night. Despite this, there have been millions of hacking attempts reported.

Using artificial intelligence (AI), a researcher has discovered two highly dangerous flaws in a programming language called PHP.

This programming language has been used in nearly 70 per cent of websites around the world.

BBC's cyber affairs correspondent, Joe Tidy, said that this is an unprecedented situation where IT teams have been scrambling to protect their organisations from a highly serious cyber attack risk, resulting in one website after another going offline.

For example, the Edinburgh Council website, the ''Doctor Who'' section of the BBC website, and websites of various companies in Japan, Belgium, and the Netherlands have been taken offline.

Even some cyber security authorities have taken their own websites offline although they were the ones trying to alert the public about its importance.

As a precaution to avoid potential risks of global cyber attacks, Bangladesh Bank has kept its website offline.

NEIR to curb illegal phones, revenue evasion
item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) plans to relaunch the National Equipment Identity Register (NEIR) in two phases from January 1 to curb annual revenue losses of around Tk2,000 crore caused by illegal mobile phone manufacturing, smuggling and unauthorised sales.
According to BSS, an assessment by the National Board of Revenue (NBR), cited in a working paper presented at a BTRC meeting, found that illegal handsets were causing significant revenue losses for the government.
Under the first phase, the core functions of NEIR will be activated, but handset deregistration will remain suspended. All currently active handsets will be registered automatically, while the IMEI details of unsold handsets held by authorised importers and domestic manufacturers will also be incorporated into the system.
The system will also include provisions to block illegal handsets imported through smuggling or tax evasion.
In the second phase, to be introduced at a later date, the BTRC plans to introduce handset deregistration to verify ownership, detect cloned devices and prevent financial fraud.
NEIR was first launched on a trial basis on July 1, 2021. However, the government later suspended automatic handset blocking and clone-prevention measures.
The NBR renewed efforts to introduce the system on October 29, 2024, followed by the Posts and Telecommunications Division on June 28, 2025.
After directives issued at an inter-ministerial meeting on December 1, 2025, and recommendations from security agencies and inter-ministerial consultations in June and July 2026, a high-level meeting chaired by the home minister on September 22 made the final recommendation to launch NEIR.
Security agencies have warned that unregistered and smuggled handsets are being used in organised crime and mobile financial service fraud, underscoring the need to introduce the system.
Meanwhile, the BTRC has approved a roadmap to phase out handsets that support only 2G networks by December 2029.

item.title: Savings accounts earn little against rising inflation
item.description:
Depositors are struggling to cope with the pressure of inflation with the interest earned from keeping money in banks.
Despite rising prices of essential commodities and living costs, several top commercial banks in the country have reduced the interest rate on one-year fixed deposits to 7.5%.
Meanwhile, the inflation rate in the country stood at 8.34% last September.
In other words, the interest earned from bank deposits is lower than the rate of inflation.
After deducting taxes and other fees, the real income of depositors drops even further.
As a result, retirees, senior citizens, and families who rely on bank interest to manage household expenses are facing the greatest pressure.
It is becoming increasingly difficult for them to meet escalating costs using returns from deposits.
Moreover, even with interest payouts, the real purchasing power of saved funds is eroding due to inflation.
Banks state that while deposits have increased, the demand for private sector loans remains low.
Consequently, they hold a massive surplus of liquidity. Under these circumstances, the need to collect new deposits at higher interest rates has diminished, prompting banks to cut deposit rates.
According to bankers, several large banks have reduced term deposit interest rates twice over the last two months.
Depending on the bank, the rate cuts range from 50 to 100 basis points.
While interest rates on one-year deposits ranged between 9% and 10.15% in July, they dropped to 8.5%–9% in August.
Recently, this rate has declined further to 7.5%–8% at several banks.
Currently, Brac Bank and Dutch-Bangla Bank are offering 7.5% interest on one-year fixed deposits.
Bankers noted that this rate stands at 7.75% at Prime Bank and 7.5% at City Bank.
This means that if a customer deposits Tk10 lakh for one year at an interest rate of 7.5%, their total interest income at the end of the year will be Tk75,000.
However, with inflation running at 8.34% over the same period, this earnings level fails to preserve the real purchasing power of saved funds against the rising prices of goods and services.
When withholding tax, excise duties, and other applicable charges are factored in, the net payout drops even lower.
Fahmida Khatun, distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), stated: "As interest rates drop, ordinary citizens—especially retired individuals—will come under pressure. This is because many rely on the interest earned from bank deposits to run their households. Given the current high inflation environment, reduced interest rates will create additional financial strain."
She added: "In a market-driven economy, interest rates depend on demand and supply. Banks with strong liquidity positions have lower demand for new deposits, creating scope to lower interest rates."
Former chief economist of Bangladesh Bank Mustafa K Mujeri remarked: "When public trust in certain banks leads to an influx of deposits, it is natural for those banks to lower interest rates. This is standard practice in a market-based system. On the positive side, it may create opportunities to lower interest rates on bank loans, which is favorable for businesses. However, earning lower returns remains a major challenge for depositors."
Deposits rise, credit demand lags
According to data from Bangladesh Bank, total liquidity in the banking sector reached Tk781,214 crore at the end of August this year.
Against this, the statutory minimum liquidity requirement was Tk339,260 crore, leaving excess liquidity in the banking sector at approximately Tk442,000 crore.
Despite holding such significant liquidity, banks are unable to disburse these funds as loans.
Due to weak private sector investment and sluggish business expansion, demand for credit remains low. As a result, a substantial portion of deposited funds remains idle or is invested in government Treasury bills and bonds.
Bankers reported that average deposit growth in the banking sector reached 11.96% over the first eight months of this year, with several top-tier banks experiencing growth between 15% and 22%.
Many customers are transferring funds from troubled banks into relatively stable institutions, leading to higher deposit concentrations in the latter.
Sohel RK Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia, stated that their bank's advance-to-deposit ratio (ADR) stands at around 60%. This indicates that lending remains low relative to deposits, leaving significant surplus funds with the bank.
Meanwhile, bankers noted that private sector credit growth has remained below 5% for over six months.
Reluctance among business owners to undertake new investments, elevated production costs, and high interest rates on loans are among the key factors driving this situation.
Banks cut interest rates to manage surplus funds
For banks, deposits represent a liability. Money collected from customers must be deployed via loans or investments to generate income.
When deposit funds cannot be disbursed as loans, banks must continue paying interest to customers without generating expected returns from those funds, pushing up fund management costs.
Under these conditions, banks are attempting to control expenses by cutting deposit interest rates.
A trend toward reducing long-term deposit rates is also emerging. Some banks are prioritizing three- to six-month short-term deposits due to uncertainty regarding future interest rate trajectories.
Additionally, declining yields on government Treasury bills and bonds are affecting banks' investment returns.
Yields on government securities generally serve as a key benchmark for broader banking sector rates.
When returns on government bills and bonds drop, banks adjust their deposit interest rates accordingly.
However, the scenario is not uniform across all financial institutions.
Some weaker banks continue to offer higher interest rates to attract deposits, creating a noticeable disparity in deposit rates across the banking sector.
Depositors are advised not to base decisions solely on high interest rate offers, but to evaluate the financial health and safety of the institution as well.
Will borrowers benefit from lower interest rates?
Banks argue that lower deposit rates will reduce their cost of funds, potentially opening up space to reduce lending rates in the future.
However, a reduction in deposit rates does not automatically guarantee a proportional drop in borrowing rates, as loan rates depend on funding costs, operational expenses, risk assessments, and broader market conditions.
Bangladesh Bank has also reduced its policy rate (repo rate) from 10% to 9.5% to encourage investment and credit flow. Nevertheless, weak credit demand in the private sector continues to leave excess liquidity unabsorbed.
According to economists, creating an investment-friendly environment is crucial to driving credit demand.
When business owners step forward to establish new factories, expand production, and generate employment, banks will have greater opportunities to direct surplus liquidity into productive sectors.
This would enhance bank revenues while re-energizing the broader economy.
Mustafa K Mujeri suggests that depositors may consider alternative investment vehicles, such as National Savings Certificates (Sanchayapatra) or the capital market.
However, while the stock market offers potential returns, it also carries the risk of financial loss. Therefore, funds should not be shifted into high-risk investments purely in pursuit of higher yields.

item.title: Targeted by Trump, ICC wins top EU rights prize
item.description:
Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month -- a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful”, arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions -- which will come into force in six months -- and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working.
“The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.
Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania’s opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

Japan to arrange $6.35 billion in private investment in Bangladesh
item.description:
Japan is expected to arrange private-sector investments worth ¥1 trillion, equivalent to around $6.35 billion, in Bangladesh over the next five years, according to a report published by Japan's Nikkei Asia newspaper.
The proposed investment arrangement is expected to be mentioned in a joint statement following a summit between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, who is scheduled to visit Japan this month, the report said.
The planned investments are expected to cover automobile and other manufacturing industries, as well as the construction of energy facilities, according to Nikkei.
The investment initiative is also expected to involve companies entering the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone, which is being developed by several parties, including Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corporation.
The proposed investment plan could open up new opportunities for Bangladesh to attract Japanese capital, expand industrial production, diversify its manufacturing base and strengthen energy infrastructure.
Japan has long been an important development partner of Bangladesh, with cooperation spanning infrastructure, trade, investment and industrial development.

France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests
item.description:
FRANCE-CRIME-INVESTIGATIONS-POLICE

France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said Friday.

President Emmanuel Macron, who according to aides is postponing a visit later this month to Nigeria and Senegal amid the crisis, held a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and was to meet security forces.

He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked the movement that has broadened into a nationwide show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.

Some 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a press conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.

The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.

Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.

Nunez was expected to visit the city Friday to "inspect the security arrangements" at the request of the prime minister's office, it said.

At Macron's meeting with students, "we will present our demands to him -- which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system," Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP.

Macron's government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.

In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.

On Thursday, Macron called for "the utmost severity" against "acts of delinquency", accusing "ultra-left" groups of having sought to "bring down the republic" last weekend.

'Police have a responsibility'

On Saturday, a second round of demonstrations is expected across France.

Lyon's city centre in the southeast will be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.

Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an "exceptional basis" -- the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.

They also reversed a decision to suspend all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.

Some 20 per cent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.

The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.

A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 per cent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.

It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 per cent of the vote.

item.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
item.description:
APPLE-IPHONE/BRITAIN

Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.

From Singapore and Shanghai to London and Berlin, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days.

Competitors such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones.

It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary".

Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online.

In Sydney, which was the first Apple store to sell the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo.

In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to six straight quarters of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices.

Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi 1810.HK, but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's first foldable.

"I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.

Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models.

Others were resellers.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked.

Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain.

"Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said.

Mixed reviews

Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.

But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers.

They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers.

"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."

In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.

"I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices."

Tough to find

Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.

IDC expects Apple will take 44 per cent of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31 per cent of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.

"Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo.

"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.

item.title: NCP: Patwary, Hasnat, Sarjis and Asif get promotion; 7 posts abolished
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP) has published a restructured 195-member committee, promoting Nasiruddin Patwary and Hasnat Abdullah to the position of senior joint convener. Sarjis Alam and Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain have also been promoted to senior joint member secretary.

Meanwhile, Samanta Sharmin and Ariful Islam Adeeb, who were senior joint conveners in the previous committee, have been made joint conveners. Abdul Hannan Masud, previously senior joint chief coordinator, has also been appointed joint convener, while Nahida Sarwar Niva, formerly senior joint member secretary, has been made joint member secretary.

The restructured committee was published on the NCP’s verified Facebook page at around 12:15 pm on Friday.

The restructuring has effectively abolished seven posts from the party’s organisational structure. These are chief coordinator, chief organiser for the northern region, chief organiser for the southern region, spokesperson, senior joint chief coordinator, organiser and joint chief coordinator.

However, the restructured committee retains two senior joint conveners and two senior joint member secretaries, as in the previous committee.

In the previous structure, Nasiruddin Patwary held the post of chief coordinator, Sarjis was chief organiser for the northern region, Hasnat was chief organiser for the southern region, Asif was spokesperson and Hannan was senior joint chief coordinator. A total of 42 people served as organisers for the northern and southern regions, while 23 held the post of joint chief coordinator.

The new committee includes 24 joint conveners and six joint member secretaries. While the previous committee had no secretarial posts, the restructured committee has assigned 32 people to 32 secretarial positions, each with one or two assistant secretaries.

In addition, the committee has 19 assistant secretaries, 58 members and 11 organising secretaries.

The NCP began its journey on 28 February 2025 with a 217-member committee. Some additions and removals were made later.

The party’s central committee has now welcomed AK Flora, granddaughter of Sher-e-Bangla AK Fazlul Huq, the first prime minister of undivided Bengal, who joined the party in April, and Ishaq Sarkar, an expelled BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) leader who is also convener of the NCP’s Dhaka South city unit.

Both have been appointed joint conveners. Tarek A Adel, a former adviser to the Jatiya Party, has also been made a joint convener of the NCP’s central committee.

The restructuring has, in effect, elevated Nasiruddin Patwary, Hasnat Abdullah, Sarjis Alam and Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain to more influential positions within the party.

Since the party’s formation, these leaders have played significant roles in the last national election and in various recent political issues. Their new positions reflect that influence.

NCP leaders familiar with the process said the leaders’ performance had been taken into consideration during the restructuring.

Three of the NCP’s eight members of parliament (MPs) are among the six top leaders in the restructured committee: convener Nahid Islam, member secretary Akhter Hossen and senior joint convener Hasnat Abdullah.

The party’s other five MPs—Abdullah Al Amin, Atiqur Rahman Mojahid, Abdul Hannan Masud, Mahmuda Alam Mitu and Nusrat Tabassum—have been appointed joint conveners.

The 11 top posts in the previous NCP committee were known as the party leadership’s “Super Eleven”. Following the restructuring, this has become the “Super Six”. The NCP, however, refers to 16 members of its political council as the “Super Sixteen”. The political council is the party’s highest policy-making body.

The 10 members of the political council outside the top six leaders are Abdullah Al Amin, Ariful Islam Adeeb, Atiqur Rahman Mojahid, Abdul Hannan Masud, Ali Ahsan Junayed, Sarwar Tushar, Akram Hossain, Salehuddin Sifat, Mahmuda Alam Mitu and Nusrat Tabassum.

item.title: PHP flaws prompt 12-hour shutdown of digital land services server
item.description:
The Ministry of Land has announced maintenance work to improve the security of its system, following the detection of security vulnerabilities in PHP.

To this end, the ministry has kept the digital land services (land.gov.bd) server shut down for 12 consecutive hours, from midnight tonight (Friday) until noon tomorrow (Saturday).

No land-related services will be available during this period, according to a press release issued by the ministry.

PHP flaws prompt millions of hacking attempts amid rush to patch vulnerabilities

The notice said the security upgrade would be carried out following an urgent cyber alert issued on 22 October by BGD e-GOV CIRT, the government agency responsible for cybersecurity.

Digital land services include mutation, payment of land development tax, collection of land records and mouza maps, land acquisition and requisition, leasing and settlement, land revenue cases, and the land information bank.

The platform also offers a calculator to determine land inheritance, land-related laws and regulations, various forms, and service guidelines.

Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks

In the press release, the ministry requested everyone not to make any payments for land services after 11:45pm on Thursday. Apologising for the temporary inconvenience, it sought everyone's cooperation in successfully completing the maintenance work.

Recently, two serious security vulnerabilities were identified in PHP, a widely used programming language for developing and operating websites.

The vulnerabilities have raised concerns about the security of websites operated by various government and commercial organisations around the world.

In response, different organisations have taken initiatives to assess and update the security of their systems.

BGD e-GOV CIRT, the government agency responsible for overseeing cybersecurity-related issues, has also issued an alert about the PHP vulnerabilities.

Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks

According to the agency's recommendations, relevant organisations must identify where PHP is being used on their servers.

They must also check whether the versions in use are vulnerable and take necessary security measures.

Earlier, the shutdown of Bangladesh Bank's server in response to the same security vulnerabilities also came to light.

This time, an initiative has been taken to update security by shutting down the digital land services server.
